final_answer:
Short answer: On the stated facts, probably yes as to the dispersal order and the arrests, but the outcome depends on facts the police could prove and on how the claim is framed. A dispersal order issued only because of generalized traffic worries and speculation about escalation, against a mostly peaceful, sign-holding crowd, is hard to justify under the First Amendment. Arrests for failure to disperse are lawful only if the underlying order was lawful and supported by probable cause.

1. Framework. A downtown plaza and sidewalks are traditional public forums. Content-neutral time, place and manner limits must be narrowly tailored to a significant interest and leave open alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989); Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965)). Speech advocating illegal action can be punished only if directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it (Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969)). Peaceful demonstrators cannot be punished merely because their message provokes hostile onlookers or because disorder is feared. Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963), reversed breach-of-peace convictions of about 187 peaceful demonstrators who refused a police dispersal order, where there was no violence or threat of violence. Collins v. Jordan, 110 F.3d 1363 (9th Cir. 1996), is persuasive authority that speculation that violence may occur does not justify banning or dispersing demonstrations. Controlling authority here is the Supreme Court and the Seventh Circuit; Collins is persuasive only.

2. Application. Facts favoring a violation: the protest was generally peaceful; entering the street occasionally and a couple of verbal arguments are not violence or a clear and present danger; the stated reasons (traffic disruption, potential for escalation) are generalized. Edwards rejects dispersal and arrest of peaceful speakers based on feared reaction. Facts favoring the City: the government has a real interest in keeping streets open, and repeated, sustained blocking of vehicle lanes can support a content-neutral order, or arrests under traffic or disorderly conduct provisions, after notice and with reasonable opportunity to comply. Illinois law supplies the relevant offenses: mob action under 720 ILCS 5/25-1 (a participant in a mob action who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer commits a Class A misdemeanor), but mob action requires force or violence disturbing the peace, or an assembly with intent to commit an offense or do violence, none of which appears on these facts; and Chicago disorderly conduct and street-obstruction ordinances, which I did not verify. A bare declaration of an 'unlawful assembly' does not make an assembly unlawful.

3. Arrests. Failure to disperse is an offense only if the order itself rested on a lawful basis. If the assembly was lawful, probable cause for the arrests is lacking, and the arrests would be both a First Amendment and Fourth Amendment violation. Individual officers may nonetheless assert qualified immunity (the question is whether clearly established law gave fair notice), and the City can be liable under 42 U.S.C. 1983 only via Monell (policy, practice or final policymaker decision). Remedies include damages, injunctive or declaratory relief, and suppression or dismissal of charges.

4. Caveats. This is a general analysis; I did not verify Seventh Circuit decisions or Chicago ordinance text, any 2025 Chicago consent decree or policy on protest dispersal, or the contemporaneous video evidence of the street entries. A court would ask how long and how substantially the street was blocked, whether the order was audible and gave a route and time to comply, and whether those arrested personally blocked traffic.

authorities.title: Collins v. Jordan
